title: Why God Allows Suffering
lead: If God is good and all-powerful, why do the innocent suffer? The question is called theodicy, from Greek words for "God" and "justice." The Bible does not give one simple answer. The book of Job stands at its center: a righteous man loses everything, refuses easy explanations, and meets God in the storm.

sections.b: Genesis traces pain and death to the first sin and the curse that followed (Genesis 3:16–19). The covenant in Deuteronomy links obedience with blessing and disobedience with disaster (Deuteronomy 28), but Joseph tells his brothers that God turned their evil into good (Genesis 50:20). The psalms of lament cry out, "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?" (Psalm 22:1) and complain that the wicked prosper (Psalm 73). Habakkuk asks why God is silent while the wicked swallow up the righteous (Habakkuk 1:13), and Ecclesiastes notes that the same fate comes to all (Ecclesiastes 9:2–3). Isaiah's servant suffers for the sins of others (Isaiah 53:4–6). Jesus denies that every disaster is a punishment for its victims (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:1–3). The apostles say suffering produces endurance (Romans 5:3–5; James 1:2–4), and Revelation promises that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).
sections.refs: Genesis 3:16–19; Deuteronomy 28:1–68; Genesis 50:20; Psalm 22:1; Psalm 73:1–28; Habakkuk 1:13; Ecclesiastes 9:2–3; Isaiah 53:4–6; Luke 13:1–5; John 9:1–3; Romans 5:3–5; James 1:2–4; Revelation 21:4

sections.b: Job is blameless, yet in the heavenly council the Accuser asks whether Job serves God for nothing, and God allows him to strike Job's wealth, children and health (Job 1–2). Job first answers, "The LORD gave, and the LORD took. Let the LORD's name be blessed" (Job 1:21). His three friends insist that suffering must come from sin; Job protests his innocence and demands a hearing with God. Elihu adds that God uses pain to warn and teach (Job 33:19–30). When the LORD answers from the storm, he does not explain the wager in heaven. He asks, "Where were you when I founded the earth?" (Job 38:4) and shows Job a world far larger than human understanding. In the end God says the friends "did not say what is right about me, the way my servant Job did" (Job 42:7). Readers have long noted that the book rejects a simple link between sin and suffering, and that it honors honest protest.

sections.h: Answers in Christian and Jewish thought
sections.b: Augustine taught that evil is not a thing God made but a lack of good, and that it entered through the misuse of free will by angels and humans. Irenaeus suggested that this world is a place where people grow toward maturity, an idea later called "soul-making." Gregory the Great's Morals on Job read Job as a picture of Christ and of the suffering church. Reformed teaching holds that God ordains all that happens, including evil, for good ends, without being the author of sin. Catholic teaching, as in John Paul II's letter Salvifici Doloris (1984), speaks of suffering joined to Christ's cross as redemptive (Colossians 1:24). Orthodox writers stress that God does not will evil, and that Christ entered suffering and death to overcome them. Maimonides read Job as a man who moved from moral goodness to true knowledge of God. After the Holocaust, many Jewish and Christian thinkers questioned any neat explanation and turned again to lament.
sections.refs: Romans 8:18–28; Colossians 1:24; 2 Corinthians 12:7–10; Hebrews 12:5–11; 1 Peter 4:12–19; Genesis 50:20

sections.h: Does God send suffering or only permit it?
sections.b: In Job's opening chapters God allows the Accuser to strike Job, yet Job says he receives bad from God as well as good (Job 2:10), and the narrator later speaks of "all the harm the LORD had brought on him" (Job 42:11). Isaiah has God say that he forms light and creates darkness (Isaiah 45:7), and 1 Kings 22:19–23 shows God sending a lying spirit. Reformed theologians tend to say God decrees suffering for wise purposes. Catholic, Orthodox, Arminian and Wesleyan writers more often say God permits evil that he does not will, and brings good out of it. Many Pentecostals stress that sickness is the work of the enemy and that God heals in answer to prayer. Open theists argue that God takes real risks with human freedom. All agree that God is not the author of sin.
sections.refs: Job 2:10; Job 42:11; Isaiah 45:7; 1 Kings 22:19–23; Amos 3:6; James 1:13; Lamentations 3:31–33

common: Most Christians hold that suffering is not always a punishment for the sufferer's own sin.
uncommon: Some thinkers, called open theists, hold that God does not plan each instance of suffering, because he has given creatures real freedom.
